intervals.label: opened as LAMPF
intervals.locator: LANL National Security Science, "Accelerating innovation" (28 Nov 2022), section on the first 800 MeV beam; rename: "In 1995, LAMPF was renamed the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center, or LANSCE"
intervals.note: The start is the month LAMPF first reached 800 MeV (9 June 1972, LANL); LANL's magazine 1663 says LAMPF "opened in 1972", and no page consulted gives a separate opening or dedication day. LANL also states that LAMPF was renamed LANSCE in 1995; that is not modeled as a separate interval (see facility aliases).
intervals.quote: on June 9, 1972, the much-anticipated energy of 800 million electron volts was achieved, making LAMPF the most powerful linear accelerator in the world at that time.

name: Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (linac)
notes: kind is `linac`; LANSCE's proton beam also feeds spallation-neutron and other secondary-beam facilities not modeled here.

beam_energy.locator: LANL page "LANL's Linear Accelerator (LINAC)", second paragraph
beam_energy.quote: The third and longest stage of the accelerator (800m) is the side-coupled-cavity linac, where particles are accelerated to their final energy of 800 MeV.

summary.plain: A long particle accelerator at Los Alamos National Laboratory that fires protons at high energy. Originally built to study the strong nuclear force, it later produced the neutrino beam for the LSND experiment and today serves nuclear-security and materials research.
summary.technical: Los Alamos Neutron Science Center linac (Technical Area 53), originally LAMPF, opened June 1972; accelerates protons to 800 MeV; its beam-stop neutrinos fed the LSND experiment.
